content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem and planning its structure. The symptom is that account pages failed for shoppers, stated without any numbers. The causal chain starts there: account page requests were failing, and the reason is that they raised a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py at line 47.

Next I'm checking the timing of the renderer switch and the legacy flag being turned off, since that looks like the trigger. I'm also ruling out the monthly-spend switch and the recent deploys, because the reverts and the deploy log don't point to them. A background run of client disconnects before the onset is on my list to check, but it's at baseline, so I'm treating it as not the cause.

I'm settling the causal chain's last step: the new renderer's spend summary divides by a count that is zero for an ordinary shopper with no purchases this month, which is why those requests failed. I'm weighing whether the monthly-spend switch belongs in the chain at all, since turning it off didn't help.

I'm settling the root cause's wording: the divisor is zero for a shopper who bought before but not this month, and turning the legacy flag off routed account pages through the new renderer's monthly path, where that division sits. I'm also checking whether the ZeroDivisionError handling in the account page hides the failure from callers.

I'm working out how to phrase the plain-language version of the cause: a setting being switched off moved account pages onto a newer rendering path that divides by zero, likely for shoppers who've bought before but nothing this month. I'm also checking how to say that the faulty division is still in the code, so turning that setting off again would fail account pages the same way.

I'm listing the contributing factors now: a production flag flip that could move every account page to the new renderer at once with no gradual rollout, and no test that covers a shopper with past purchases but none this month on the monthly path. I still need to tie the test gap to an action item in the record.

I'm now weighing the third contributing factor: nobody was paged, so the alert never reached an on-call person before the failures spread.

I'm weighing whether the alert should have paged someone, since the failures went unnoticed until a passer-by mentioned them in the thread. I'm also noting that two flag changes landed at the same instant from the same admin, which made it hard to tell which one caused the problem and led to reverting the wrong flag first.

I'm working through the action items now, starting with the rollout: the flag change should move traffic gradually by percentage and roll back automatically if the error rate rises, which addresses the factor that a single flip sent every account page to the new renderer at once. I'm also drafting a second item to require a test run of any path a flag enables before the flag is switched.

I'm working through the remaining action items: a pre-change check that a flag's code path passes its tests before the flag can be flipped in production, an on-call page on the io-shop error-rate alert, and spacing out flag changes on io-shop so they aren't made at the same instant. I'm also weighing whether keeping the legacy flag on until the fix is merged belongs in the list, and noting that the monthly-spend feature was switched back on.

I'm reviewing the lessons section now: the Mitigation Agent putting monthly-spend-feature back on once reverting it didn't help, the legacy-checkout-fallback revert and the confirmation that the alert stopped firing, the Investigator Agent's reading of the metrics, changes, and logs, and the draft fix PR #432 from the Code-Fix Agent.

I'm noting the person's lead in the thread pointed to the right flag, and that the Investigator ranked monthly-spend-feature first even though the logs already showed account pages on the new renderer. I'm also checking whether anything went well by luck, though nothing stands out yet.

I'm weighing whether the lead in the thread counted for anything here. It didn't change the sequence of actions, since the investigation ranked the legacy fallback second and Argus reverted the monthly-spend feature first, so the right flag was only tried after the first revert was refuted. Still, the lead turned out to be correct.

I'm checking the assumptions behind the timeline, including the placeholder in the log lines and whether the log covers every request. I'm also working out what sets the monthly path, and noting that turning monthly-spend-feature off didn't help, so the new renderer likely reaches the faulty division regardless.

I'm checking the deploy history for the day before the onset, which turned up nothing, and noting that the client-disconnect errors stop before the failures begin while the ZeroDivisionError errors start right at the onset. I'm also tracking which flag states were in effect at the start of the incident window, with the onset dated to the first flag change.

I'm now checking the timing of account pages moving to the new renderer from 17:43 onward, and the ZeroDivisionError errors that ran over the following few minutes at spend_summary.py:47. action_items.item: Keep legacy-checkout-fallback ON until the fix proposed in draft pull request #432 is merged.
Roll out flags that move traffic to a new code path, such as legacy-checkout-fallback, by percentage, with automatic rollback when the error rate rises.
Require the tests of the code path a flag turns on to pass, including shoppers with past purchases but none this month for the spend summary, before that flag can be changed in production.
Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call page.
Require flag changes on io-shop to be made one at a time, with the error rate watched before the next change is made.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed, and the share of requests failing rose well above its usual level.
Account page requests were raising ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py at line {F1.1}, logged over {G5309.3}. The ClientDisconnected failures logged before then stop at {G46bc.3}.

Account pages had moved from the legacy renderer to the new renderer, which served the most pages at {Gc27d.11}. The flag reads show legacy-checkout-fallback mostly off at {G7ad6.6} and off over {G7037.4}.

ruled_out.what: The monthly-spend-feature flag, switched on by admin at the same instant: turning it back off left the service at the incident's level, so it was put back on.
A deploy: no deploys came back for the day before the onset.
The ClientDisconnected failures: they were logged only before the onset, and the failures from the onset on are ZeroDivisionError.

causal_chain.step: The feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off by admin at {P1.1}. Turning it back on brought the service out of the incident's level.
The new renderer's spend summary divides by a count that is zero for an ordinary shopper with no purchases this month, so its requests for those shoppers failed.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching off a setting moved shoppers' account pages onto a newer way of building them, and that newer way crashed by dividing by zero, likely for shoppers who have bought before but have bought nothing yet this month.

contributing_factors.factor: One flag change could move every account page from the legacy renderer to the new renderer at once. No gradual rollout or automatic rollback was seen on legacy-checkout-fallback.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A gradual, percentage-based rollout with rollback on error rate would have exposed only a small share of account pages to the failing path, and it would have been undone automatically.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that ran the new renderer's spend summary against a shopper with past purchases but none this month before the flag change sent account pages to it. Code-Fix says its new tests for that case would fail against the current code.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Such a check would likely have failed before legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off, and the change would have been held back.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was linked to no on-call incident, so nobody was paged.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: An on-call person would have been engaged on the alert and could have acted on the switched-off flag alongside Argus.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: Admin made two flag changes on the service at the same instant, so the record could not tell which one set off the errors.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: With only one change at the onset, the right flag would have been reverted first and the service restored without first trying the wrong one.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

lead_effects.effect: It did not change what was done: the investigation weighed it as unverified and ranked legacy-checkout-fallback second, so Argus reverted that flag only after the monthly-spend-feature revert was refuted, and the confirmed action then bore the lead out.

went_well.item: A person in the incident's thread named legacy-checkout-fallback, the flag the confirmed action later showed was the one that mattered.
The Investigator Agent read the metrics, the production changes and the logs, and formed candidate causes that covered both flag changes.
The Mitigation Agent put monthly-spend-feature back ON once reverting it did not help, so no unneeded change was left in place.
The Mitigation Agent turned legacy-checkout-fallback back ON.
The Mitigation Agent confirmed that the service was no longer at the incident's level.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #432.

went_wrong: The investigation ranked monthly-spend-feature first and Argus reverted it first. Yet the logs it had read showed account pages moving from the legacy renderer to the new renderer at the onset, and a person in the thread had named legacy-checkout-fallback, so the flag that restored the service was reverted only after the first revert was refuted.

input.root_cause: In `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, the monthly spend summary divides the account's total for the month by the number of purchases it made this month (line {F1.1}). That number is zero for an ordinary shopper who has bought before but not this month. Switching legacy-checkout-fallback off sent account pages to the new renderer, whose spend summary reaches this division, and `serve_account_page` turns the resulting ZeroDivisionError into a failed page.
input.still_at_risk: Switching the legacy-checkout-fallback flag off again would send account pages back to the new renderer and fail them again.
